lessonRef.title: Word work and decoding focus: syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split within the unit “Word Builders: Syllables, Prefixes, Suffixes, and Roots.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's word work and decoding focus work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
A long word is often a short word wearing extra pieces. Once a reader learns the pieces, the long word stops being frightening.

Some pieces go on the front. Un means not, so unkind means not kind and unlocked means not locked. Re means again, so retell means tell again and rebuild means build again. Pre means before, so preheat means heat before. Dis often works like un, so disagree means not agree.

Other pieces go on the end. Ful means full of, so hopeful means full of hope. Less means without, so hopeless means without hope. Notice that hopeful and hopeless share the same small word and point in opposite directions. Ly usually tells how something is done, so slowly tells how a person walked. Ness turns a describing word into a thing, so kindness is the quality of being kind.

A few endings come to English from Latin, and they show up constantly in school books. Ment makes a thing out of an action, as in payment, movement, and agreement. Tion and sion do something similar, as in action, invention, and decision. Able means can be, as in washable and readable.

The useful move is always the same. When a word looks too long, cover the front piece and the end piece with a finger and read what is left. If the middle is a word you know, put the pieces back one at a time and check whether the meaning still fits the sentence.

This will not work on every word. English borrowed from too many places to be perfectly tidy. But it works often enough that a reader who tries it will get through most long words without help, and getting through without help is the whole point.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Parts That Change a Word”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Parts That Change a Word,” then answer: Choose two words or sentence parts in the reading that matter to syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split. How does each part shape meaning?

Deliverable: Grade 3: a two-entry word-and-meaning annotation; write 3–5 complete sentences.

Evidence requirement: Use one exact detail. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split is not yet secure, return to “The Parts That Change a Word” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply syllable patterns and where a longer word can be split to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Parts That Change a Word.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
